item.title: Izumo Dome: A Giant Wooden Dome and Science Fun — Guide
item.description: The Izumo Dome is one of the largest wooden-frame domes in Japan, a vast circular hall near Izumo whose lattice of local cedar timber supports a translucent membrane roof, filling the interior with soft natural light. Built as an all-weather multipurpose space, it hosts sports, community events and markets, and offers family-friendly play and hands-on activities that make it a useful stop with children, especially on a wet or cold day when outdoor sights are less appealing.

item.title: Mojiko Retro District, Kitakyushu — Guide
item.description: Mojiko, at the northern tip of Kyushu in Kitakyushu, was once one of Japan’s busiest international trading ports, and its historic heart is preserved as the charming ‘Mojiko Retro’ district. Around the harbour stand a cluster of elegant Western-style buildings from the Meiji and Taisho eras — a former customs house, the old Moji railway station, trading company offices and a striking former bank — their retro architecture beautifully lit at night.

item.title: Namba Parks: The Terraced Rooftop Garden of Namba — Guide
item.description: Namba Parks is a shopping and office complex built above the old Nankai stadium site next to Namba Station, but it is far more interesting than that suggests. Designed by the American architect Jon Jerde to resemble a natural canyon, its floors step back as they rise, and across their setbacks climbs Parks Garden — a continuous rooftop park of some eight levels, planted with hundreds of species of trees, shrubs and flowers, with lawns, streams and quiet corners.

item.title: Teshima Art Museum: A Space of Water and Light — Guide
item.description: The Teshima Art Museum, on the peaceful island of Teshima near Naoshima, is one of the most extraordinary museums in the world — though it contains just a single, endlessly changing work. Designed by architect Ryue Nishizawa with artist Rei Naito, the building is a vast, curving white concrete shell shaped like a water droplet, with two large oval openings to the sky. Inside there are no paintings or objects; instead, tiny droplets of water seep continuously from the floor, forming, merging, trickling and pooling in a slow, mesmerising dance, while wind, birdsong and light enter from above.

item.title: Tokyo Station & Marunouchi — Guide
item.description: Tokyo Station’s Marunouchi side is one of the city’s most striking architectural sights: a magnificent red-brick Renaissance-style building originally opened in 1914 and beautifully restored to its original form, with elegant domes and a stately facade that lights up handsomely at night. Far more than a place to catch a train, the station is a vast destination in itself, with an enormous underground world of shopping streets and restaurants — including ‘Tokyo Character Street’ (with shops for popular anime and TV characters), ‘Tokyo Ramen Street’ (gathering famous ramen shops), sweets streets and countless eateries.

item.title: Tottori Prefectural Museum of Art — Guide
item.description: The Tottori Prefectural Museum of Art is the prefecture’s flagship art museum, a strikingly modern building in Kurayoshi in central Tottori that has quickly become a cultural anchor for the region. Its collection and changing exhibitions span the art of Tottori and the wider San’in region alongside modern and contemporary Japanese and international works, and its architecture — light-filled, open and designed as a public gathering space as much as a gallery — is part of the appeal.

item.title: Nakanoshima Guide: Osaka's Riverside Island of Art & Architecture
item.description: A long, slender island between two rivers in the heart of Osaka, Nakanoshima is the city’s most refined district — a calm, green ribbon of historic architecture, art museums, and riverside promenades that feels worlds away from the noise of Minami. Here the stately red-brick Osaka City Central Public Hall anchors a cluster of galleries, a famous rose garden, leafy walkways, and stylish waterside cafes. It’s where Osaka comes to slow down, stroll, and look at art and the water.

item.title: Umeda Sky Building Guide: The Floating Garden Observatory
item.description: One of Osaka’s boldest pieces of architecture, the Umeda Sky Building is two 40-storey towers joined at the top by a doughnut-shaped Floating Garden Observatory seemingly suspended in mid-air. Glass escalators cross the open void between the towers to reach the rooftop, where an open-air deck gives a 360-degree panorama over the whole of Osaka — spectacular at sunset and after dark. Frequently listed among the world’s great buildings, it’s the city’s best skyline viewpoint and an experience in itself.
